ECB: two candidates remain to succeed Lagarde, Spain's Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Knot, and ministers want to settle three posts at once

With applications closed on November 6, two names remain to replace Christine Lagarde at the head of the European Central Bank: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot. Meeting on Monday, November 9, eurozone finance ministers also discussed two other seats to fill, those of Isabel Schnabel and Philip Lane [1][2][6].
Christine Lagarde announced on October 29 that she would leave the ECB presidency on February 7, 2027, nine months before the end of her term [2][3].
The application deadline, set for November 6 by Eurogroup president Kyriakos Pierrakakis, produced only two names: Pablo Hernández de Cos, for Spain, and Klaas Knot, for the Netherlands [1][6].
Pablo Hernández de Cos has headed the Bank for International Settlements since July 2025 and was governor of the Bank of Spain; Klaas Knot chaired the Dutch central bank from 2011 to 2025 [2][6].

For Madrid, Deputy Prime Minister Carlos Cuerpo said he was "confident" that his compatriot would bring to the ECB "the same steady hand and inspiring leadership" (translated from English) [11]; both candidates have the official backing of their government [5].

On Monday, November 9, eurozone ministers reviewed the applications. Kyriakos Pierrakakis said that three appointments could be considered together to "ease consensus": the presidency, Isabel Schnabel's seat on the Executive Board (vacant in January) and the post of chief economist, whose holder Philip Lane ends his term on May 31 [2][4].

According to Xinhua, Germany wants to keep Schnabel's seat and France is aiming for the chief economist post; Reuters notes that this seat should go to Germany, France or Italy, which effectively hold one permanently [2][4].

The final decision rests with the European Council, after the Eurogroup's recommendation and consultation of the ECB and the European Parliament, by an enhanced qualified majority of eurozone countries; the aim would be an appointment at the heads of state and government summit in December [2][9].

Key takeaway: choosing the next ECB boss is as much a political decision as a monetary one, and it will be made as a package with two other seats, with each large country wanting to keep its place [2][4].

Knot describes himself as a "hawk", that is, a supporter of a rather tough interest-rate policy to fight inflation, while expert surveys list Hernández de Cos among the favorites; an OMFIF survey in April had three candidates tied [5][7].

The stakes are concrete: the ECB sets interest rates for the 21 eurozone countries [6]. Inflation there rose to 4.0% in October, its highest level in three years, and the ECB is moving closer to a rate hike in December, according to CNBC [10]. The future president will inherit this issue when taking office in February 2027.

Another post is already filled: Croatia's Boris Vujčić has been named ECB vice-president to replace Luis de Guindos [8]. The appointment of the leadership team will therefore happen in several stages, and it is only in December that we will know who takes the helm of the central bank [2][8][9].

The ECB decides the interest rates that set the cost of your mortgage or your student loan in euros, and it monitors prices across the eurozone. Depending on whether the next president leans more or less toward high rates, credit may cost more or less. We are at the application stage: nothing is decided before December, and this is not financial advice.

France: Lecornu brings forward the minimum wage to 1,502 euros net from December 1, but unions and employers both call the response bad, each for the opposite reason

On Monday, November 9, at the end of the social conference at Matignon, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced a boost to the minimum wage (Smic): +1.6% from December 1 instead of January 1, or about 1,502 euros net per month. The CGT calls it "crumbs", the Medef a "bad response" [1][2][4][6].

On Monday, November 9, after the social conference held at Matignon with unions and employers, Sébastien Lecornu announced that the Smic would be raised by 1.6% from December 1, 2026, rather than January 1, 2027, to reach about 1,502 euros net per month [1][2].
The increase amounts to about 24 euros more net each month [2][4]. The Prime Minister presents it as "the second largest increase in twenty years" [4].
The Smic had already been raised by 2.4% on June 1, 2026 to keep up with inflation [8]: December 1 will therefore be the second increase of the year [1][8].

Lecornu also wants to restart wage negotiations in the industry sectors: according to Boursorama, one sector in two has not renegotiated its pay scale in ten years, and 69 sectors still have minimums below the Smic. A wage monitoring committee, bringing together unions and employers' organizations, is to be set up in the coming days [3].

A decree expected this week is meant to make the calculation of social-contribution exemptions less favorable in sectors whose minimums remain below the Smic [3]. According to ICI, the fuel aid is also extended [1].

On the union side, the CFDT calls the increase "insufficient" (it was asking for 100 euros per month), even though its general secretary Marylise Léon welcomes the fact that aid to companies is made conditional on sector-level negotiations; the CGT of Sophie Binet speaks of "crumbs" (it was asking for about 150 euros) and announces a new strike day [4][5].

Olivier Faure, for the Socialist Party, says "it doesn't add up" [5]; on the right, Laurent Wauquiez instead calls for a cut in public spending [4]. Patrick Martin, president of the Medef, replies: "We are bringing a bad answer to a real problem", and fears that the rise in the wage bill will push labor-intensive companies into the red [6].

Key takeaway: the government gives minimum-wage workers a bit of purchasing power, but it convinces neither those who wanted more nor those who pay the bill, which leaves the social conflict open [4][5][6].

How it works: the Smic is the legal minimum wage. It is raised with inflation, and the government can add a "coup de pouce" (a boost), that is, a larger or earlier increase than the rule requires. The reports do not agree on the exact size of this boost: Boursorama speaks of 0.6% added to the automatic revaluation brought forward by a month, the other sources of 1.6% in total [1][3][4].

The stakes go beyond the Smic itself. When the minimum wage rises, the pay scales of sectors whose minimums are below it get caught up by the law, hence the government's insistence on the 69 sectors concerned and on the decree linking contribution relief to wage negotiations [3][4].

Politically, tension remains high. After the November 5 strike, Basta reports that the announcements were enough to divide the union front, which is now calling for the November 17 strike in scattered order, and that civil service unions will be received separately on Friday [7]. Employers, for their part, fear the cost of an increase that adds to other charges [6].

If you are paid the minimum wage full time, you will receive about 24 euros more net per month from December. If you are just above it, your sector may be pushed to renegotiate its pay scales, which could affect your salary. For a small shop or a restaurant, the bill goes up: that is the fear expressed by the Medef. Nothing is recommended here: this is a snapshot of the situation.

Social security budget: the Senate wants to index pensions up to 1,500 euros, where the government stops at 1,260, without touching the 12.7 billion deficit

Having received the 2027 social security budget that the National Assembly rejected, the Senate is preparing its version: the social affairs committee wants to raise from 1,260 to 1,500 euros the threshold for pensions revalued in January, while committing to hold the 12.7 billion euro deficit sought by the government. Formal vote on November 18 [1][2][3][5].

The National Assembly rejected the draft 2027 social security budget (PLFSS): the committee turned it down, then the revenue section was rejected on the floor by 115 votes to 1 with 22 abstentions, which amounts to rejecting the whole text; the Senate therefore receives the version tabled by the government on October 1 [4].
In that version, Article 35 limits the January 2027 pension increase to pensions whose total does not exceed 1,260 euros per month [4].

The Senate's social affairs committee, chaired by Philippe Mouiller, proposes raising this threshold to 1,500 euros, with inflation indexation for pensions up to that level; this would reduce by about 200 million euros the 4 billion euros in savings expected from the measure [1][2].
The senators also want to remove certain new levies, such as the contribution on medical devices [2].
Philippe Mouiller committed his committee to "hold the deficit level" of the government: 12.7 billion euros in 2027, against 21.8 billion in 2026 [2][3].
Without a voted budget, a special law would simply renew existing funding and push the deficit to 22.6 billion euros, according to the Senate [3].

The Senate's formal vote on the whole text is scheduled for Wednesday, November 18. Sébastien Lecornu has promised, according to AFP, not to use Article 49.3 or ordinances if there is no parliamentary obstruction [5].

Key takeaway: retirees are at the heart of the trade-off, between a 4 billion euro saving from raising only pensions up to 1,260 euros and a threshold raised to 1,500 euros that protects more small pensions [1][2][4].

How it works: every January 1, pensions are in principle adjusted for inflation. By limiting this increase to the smallest ones, the state saves on one of social security's biggest expenses. The higher the threshold, the more retirees are protected and the less the state saves: here, 200 million euros out of 4 billion, or 5% of the planned saving [1][2].
The deficit is the other issue: it would fall from 21.8 to 12.7 billion euros, almost by half, through measures two-thirds of which rely on spending, according to a Senate summary [3].

The Senate plays a counterweight role: it takes up the government's text without rejecting it, but corrects its most sensitive measures, pensions and the tax on medical devices. It remains to be seen whether the Assembly, which had rejected everything, will accept this compromise, or whether the government will look for another route [1][2][5].

If your grandparents have a pension between 1,260 and 1,500 euros per month, they are affected: with the government's version it would not keep up with inflation in January; with the Senate's it would. For you, social security funds health care and pensions: its deficit is one day repaid through contributions, taxes or savings.

Brussels: the EU has until November 16 to wrap up its 2027 budget, and its tobacco tax awaits Sweden's agreement

EU finance ministers met on Monday, November 9 (Ecofin), then on Tuesday the 10th for the budget. Two files are pressing: the 2027 budget, to be concluded by midnight on November 16 at the latest, and European tobacco taxation, which requires the unanimity of the 27 and which Sweden refuses as it stands for nicotine pouches [1][2][3][4].

The economy and finance ministers of the 27 met in Brussels on Monday, November 9 (Ecofin), ahead of a budget Council on Tuesday the 10th [2][6]. On the agenda: a political agreement on the tobacco taxation package, the report on the G20 finance meeting in Bangkok on October 15 and a debate on the economic impact of Russia's war against Ukraine [2][3].

For the 2027 budget, the Council's position sets 191.88 billion euros in commitments and 202.07 billion in payments, excluding special instruments; the European Parliament is asking for 194 billion in commitments [1].

The Council and Parliament must agree by midnight on November 16 at the latest [1]. 2027 is the seventh and last year of the 2021-2027 multiannual financial framework, while member states negotiate the 2028-2034 long-term budget in parallel [1].

On tobacco, a Council secretariat note dated November 5 leaves it to ministers to decide the minimum applicable to nicotine pouches: 10% of the retail price or 30 euros per kilo from January 1, 2028 [3].

Sweden, which refuses a minimum above 20 euros per kilo for pouches, is the main obstacle, according to a European official quoted by Law360: the Commission originally proposed 71.50 euros per kilo, and a May 29 compromise mentioned 30 euros for 2028-2029 [4][5].

Traditional Swedish snus remains excluded from the draft, but tobacco-free nicotine pouches would enter the harmonized framework; the vote had been postponed from October to November to give Stockholm time to form a government after the September 13 elections [4][5].
At the time of writing, no official report of the November 9 Ecofin had yet been published: the outcome of the meeting remains to be confirmed [2].
Key takeaway: the EU's annual budget has a deadline, November 16, and the tobacco tax can be blocked by a single country, because EU tax decisions require the unanimity of the 27 [1][4].

How it works for the budget: each autumn, the Council (the governments) and the European Parliament negotiate the following year's budget. Their positions differ by about 2 billion euros in commitments (191.88 against 194): the agreement is built through mutual concessions before the legal deadline [1].

For the tobacco tax, the aim is to harmonize minimum tax levels across the EU, which the Commission wanted higher for new nicotine products. Sweden defends the freedom to set its own rates according to the risk of each product and refuses to go above 20 euros per kilo [4][5].

This is not the first time the file has stalled: it had already been postponed from October to November. As long as the 27 do not agree, no European rule changes, and each country keeps its own rates [4][5].

The EU budget funds, among other things, farm aid, regional funds and research: a prolonged disagreement can delay payments. On tobacco, the European tax targets tobacco and nicotine products; as long as the 27 do not agree, nothing changes in the prices you pay.

news.2026-11-10-tchequie-budget-2027-def: Czechia: the 2027 budget provides for a deficit of 386 billion crowns, the country's second-heaviest ever

Andrej Babiš's government has adopted a 2027 budget with a deficit of about 386 billion crowns (18 billion dollars), against 310 billion this year. The text passed its first reading in Parliament on October 22; the opposition called for a no-confidence vote [2][3].

Revenue is forecast at 2,199 billion crowns (+3.9%) and spending at 2,585 billion (+6.5%): spending is rising faster than revenue [2]. Some sources cite a deficit of 389 billion, depending on the version of the draft [1][4].
Debt service would rise from 110 billion crowns this year to 130 billion in 2027 [2].
Prime Minister Andrej Babiš had promised a deficit "well below 400 billion"; the government justifies the borrowing by investment, health care, pensions and civil servants' pay [1][3].
Economist Jan Berka (Portu platform) judges this deficit too high for the state of the economy, according to the ČTK agency [2][3].
Key takeaway: Czechia is spending clearly faster than it takes in, and this choice is becoming both a political and a market issue [1][3].
A heavier deficit forces the state to borrow more: debt and its interest grow, and analysts quoted by the Czech press fear slightly higher interest rates, and therefore more expensive mortgages [4].
It is an example of an EU country choosing to borrow more to invest, at a time when France is also debating its debt and deficit.
The Chamber of Deputies must still adopt the 2027 budget after the October 22 first reading [2].

news.2026-11-10-bulgarie-deficit-2027-ra: Bulgaria: under pressure from Brussels, the Radev government tightens its 2027 deficit target, after 5.7% of GDP in 2026

Bulgaria, which joined the eurozone this year, adopted a 2026 budget with a deficit of 5.7% of GDP, almost double the European limit of 3%. For 2027, Prime Minister Rumen Radev promises a reduction and sees it as "a strong argument" against possible EU sanctions [1][3][4].
The government adopted the 2026 budget with a deficit of 5.7% of GDP, almost double the European limit of 3% [4][5].
The 2027 draft sent to the Commission cuts the deficit by 0.8 points, to 4.3% of GDP, with less spending but also less revenue relative to the economy [2].

A November 2 letter to the Commission would set, according to the press, targets of about 5% for 2026, 4.2% for 2027 and 3.5% for 2028; the figures vary from one document to another and need to be confirmed against the text [3].

Rumen Radev, whose Progressive Bulgaria coalition has 131 of 240 members of parliament, does not need the opposition to pass the budget; he believes the 2027 budget will be "a strong argument" against sanctions under the excessive deficit procedure [1][3].
Key takeaway: Bulgaria must show Brussels that it is keeping to its budget path shortly after adopting the euro [3][4].

An excessive deficit procedure requires a country whose deficit exceeds 3% of GDP to present a correction plan; a credible budget can avoid sanctions. Since the figures cited do not all agree, it is the trajectory (from 5.7% toward below 4.5%) that matters [1][2][3].
Bulgaria is part of the eurozone: its budget discipline affects the credibility of the common currency that you use too.

news.2026-11-10-autriche-deficit-2026-20: Austria: a deficit of 4.1% of GDP in 2026, 3.6% forecast in 2027, and a European procedure running until 2028

Austria's finance ministry expects a public deficit of 4.1% of GDP in 2026, then 3.6% in 2027, with the goal of returning to 3% in 2028. The country has been under the European excessive deficit procedure since July 2025, and research institutes see things a little more gloomily [1][2][3].

According to the finance ministry, the public deficit would be 4.1% of GDP in 2026 and 3.6% in 2027; debt would be 82.4% of GDP in 2026. It judges the budget to be on the right track, but with no financial room for maneuver [1].
The Wifo and IHS institutes forecast 4.0% in 2026 and 3.7% in 2027, with debt rising to as much as 84% of GDP [1][3].
The excessive deficit procedure was opened in July 2025; the European Commission set 2028 as the deadline to correct the deficit [1][3].

Chancellor Christian Stocker assures that the 2027-2028 "double budget" will take Austria out of this procedure, without a wealth tax or an inheritance tax and without an increase in property tax [2].
Key takeaway: Austria is an example of a eurozone country that must reduce a deficit above the 3% limit without breaking weak growth [1][3].

An excessive deficit procedure imposes a correction timetable: as long as the country sticks to it, Brussels takes no sanction. The figures from the state and the institutes differ by a few tenths of a point, which leaves little margin if the economy deteriorates [1][3].
Like France, Austria is under European constraint on its deficit: this gives a point of comparison for understanding French budget debates.
